title: Throwing matched mugs to consistent weight
subtitle: The techniques for producing a set of mugs that match in height, diameter, and wall weight
excerpt: Throwing a matched set of mugs requires controlling three variables simultaneously: the weight of clay per mug, the opening dimensions, and the pulling height. This tutorial covers the production-throwing approach to matching: weighing clay, using guide marks on a measurement stick, and checking each mug against a reference mug before cutting from the bat.
sourceNotes: Production-throwing technique for matched sets synthesised from studio ceramics functional ware instruction. Weight-and-measure methodology documented in production ceramics practice.

content.text: This technique requires a pottery wheel and kiln firing. The matching approach described assumes a set of six or more mugs thrown in a single session. Throwing matched mugs across multiple sessions introduces clay moisture and body variation that makes matching harder.

The most common mistake in production throwing is relying on feel alone. Feel drifts over the course of a session as your hands tire and your attention shifts. The production-throwing discipline uses two tools to offset this: a kitchen scale to weigh each clay ball before throwing, and a simple
throwing gauge
to check height and rim diameter after each mug. The combination catches drift before it compounds across the set.
Setting up for matched production

Make a throwing gauge from a strip of card or a thin dowel. Mark on it: the target finished height of the mug (say, 9.5 cm), and the target interior rim diameter (8 cm for a standard mug). Keep this gauge at the side of the wheel and use it after every mug.

Throw one reference mug at the start of the session and set it aside on a shelf to the left of the wheel. Every subsequent mug is compared against this reference. Check height with the gauge; check rim diameter with calipers.

Weigh each clay ball on a kitchen scale before throwing. For a 9.5 cm mug with 5 mm walls, the target wet weight per mug is 430 to 450 g. Set the scale beside the wheel and weigh every ball: even after 20 mugs, even when you are confident.
Throwing each mug
Centre the weighed ball. A consistent centring technique reduces the time per mug significantly: develop a repeatable centring sequence and use the same number of passes for each piece.
Centring
should take no more than 60 to 90 seconds per mug in a production session.
Open to 7 cm interior diameter: slightly narrower than the target rim diameter of 8 cm, which will be achieved at the top of the final pull.
Pull in three passes. After the final
pull
, hold the throwing gauge next to the mug while the wheel turns: check height against the height mark and check that the rim diameter matches the reference mug by eye or calipers.

Correct height: if the mug is too short (clay squashed, not enough pulls), return to pulling. If too tall (common in early-session mugs when hands are fresher), compress the rim very gently downward by 5 mm while the wheel turns slowly.
Compress and finish the rim. Cut from the bat.
Handles at leather-hard
At
leather-hard

, pull handles from clay of the same weight for each mug (typically 60 to 80 g per handle). Set the handle length against the reference mug before attaching: use calipers to measure the distance between upper and lower attachment points and set the same distance on every mug in the set.
What counts as matched

Handmade mugs in a set will not be identical. Matched means variation within acceptable bounds: height within ±3 mm; rim diameter within ±4 mm; finished weight after firing within ±30 g. These tolerances are tight enough that the set reads as a set on a shelf without any mug clearly standing out as the wrong height or too heavy.

rows.problem: Mugs drift taller through the session
rows.cause: Hands tired; less resistance in pulling; or clay slightly wetter as session progresses and the bucket water warms
rows.fix: Check height against the gauge after every mug. Use fresh cold water for lubrication throughout.

rows.problem: Wall thickness uneven: one side thinner than the other
rows.cause: Off-centre clay; pulling pressure inconsistent between hands
rows.fix: Spend more time on centring before pulling. Equal pressure from inside and outside hands on each pull pass.

rows.problem: Matching breaks down at mugs 15 to 20 in a longer session
rows.cause: Fatigue drift; clay drying conditions changing
rows.fix: Take a 5-minute break. Re-check the reference mug. Throw another reference mug to represent the new starting point of the second half of the session.
